# Maria's Story

Maria sits in the waiting room of the clinic with her hands folded in her lap, her posture rigid despite the comfortable chairs. At thirty-four, she carries herself with the controlled stillness of someone accustomed to maintaining composure in high-stress environments. Her dark hair is pulled back tightly, and she wears the kind of practical clothing—dark pants, a neutral blouse—that suggests she's come directly from her shift at the correctional facility where she works as a guard.

She has been in the United States for twelve years, but the journey here remains the clearest memory of her life. Maria was twenty-two when she fled El Salvador with her younger brother after their neighborhood became too dangerous. Their family had received threats from gang members, and their father had been killed in a case of mistaken identity three years prior. The decision to leave was made in a matter of hours.

The border crossing was not what she expected. Maria and her brother traveled with a coyote through the desert, but the group was intercepted by smugglers who demanded additional money. When her brother tried to run, he was beaten. Maria watched from a distance, frozen, unable to help him. She paid the smugglers everything they demanded—money borrowed from relatives, her grandmother's jewelry. The image of her brother on the ground, blood on his face, returns to her without warning.

They made it across, eventually reaching relatives in Texas. Maria worked cleaning houses, then retail, slowly building a stable life. She married Jorge, a good man who works in construction, eight years ago. They have no children yet, though they've talked about it. Five years ago, she became a prison guard—the job offered stability, benefits, and a sense of purpose. She was good at it, or so she thought.

Now, at night, she cannot sleep. She lies beside Jorge, her body tense, listening to every sound in the house. When he reaches for her in bed, she sometimes flinches before she recognizes him. She's embarrassed by this, though Jorge never complains. During her shifts at the facility, she finds herself hypervigilant in ways that feel excessive even for that environment. She notices every movement, every potential threat. Her colleagues have mentioned that she seems wound tight, but she brushes off their concerns.

Three months ago, an incident at work triggered something deeper. A young detainee—not much older than her brother was during their crossing—got into a fight with another inmate. Maria was there when the violence erupted. She didn't freeze this time; she responded professionally, as trained. But afterward, she couldn't stop shaking. That night, she had a nightmare so vivid she woke up gasping, convinced she was back in the desert, that the sounds she heard were the coyote and his men.

Since then, the nightmares have intensified. She experiences intrusive thoughts throughout the day—sudden, unwanted memories of the border crossing that pull her attention away from the present moment. At work, she's become irritable with inmates and staff alike. She snaps at minor infractions. She's started taking longer routes home from work to avoid the highway that reminds her of the desert landscape. She drinks wine most evenings, telling herself it helps her relax, though she's aware it's becoming a habit.

What troubles her most is the feeling that she's losing control. The woman who survived that crossing, who built a life, who became a professional—that woman feels increasingly distant. Maria is here because Jorge suggested it, gently but firmly. She's not sure therapy will help, but she's willing to try. She doesn't want to feel this way anymore, trapped between two worlds, unable to fully inhabit either one.
